idiom_name: private members + companion-scoped factory; opaque type alias so outsiders cannot name the resource
implementation_notes: Scala's guard is a class whose state is private ('Private members are only visible to the class/trait itself and to its companion object'; constructor parameters without val/var are private values), with public methods that consult the policy before touching the resource; the companion object is the sanctioned widening point and works as the trusted owner that builds the guard and holds the policy. Where the resource must be shared but only through the guard, a Scala 3 opaque type alias hides the representation entirely: inside the defining scope the alias is transparent, outside it 'is seen as an abstract type that has nothing to do with' the underlying representation, and the type checker enforces the abstraction at no runtime cost. Both mechanisms are compile-time walls rather than a security boundary, and Scala 3 has dropped private[this]/protected[this]; the compiler infers the same restriction for private members used only through this and may then elide the field, which matters to reflective/serialization access.
pitfalls: Companion access is a deliberate hole in the class's privacy: code in the companion object reads the resource directly, so keep privileged logic there minimal (construction, key handling) instead of moving operations into it.

Scala 3 may compile a private val that is only used via this without a backing field; reflection or serialization then behaves differently - declare the field qualified-private when a framework must see it.

Opaque types are compile-time only: equality is mapped to the underlying type after type checking and the alias cannot be private, so code inside the defining scope still reaches the representation - good for API abstraction, not for confining hostile code.
private[pkg]/protected[pkg] qualifications are easy to widen while fixing a compile error; treat each widening as a design change, because it makes the resource nameable across the package.
